title: Before the Trees
text: Imagine stepping out of a time machine onto dry land over four hundred million years ago. The first thing you notice is the silence.

title: Before the Trees
text: There are no birds in the branches above you, no rustling leaves, and no flowers along the hills.
nxt: In fact, there is nothing overhead at all.

title: Before the Trees

nxt: If you look down at your boots, the plant life barely reaches your ankles.

title: Before the Trees

title: The Stone Pillars
text: You turn toward the horizon, and your eyes catch something impossible.
nxt: Rising from the flat, rock-strewn plain are massive, stone-colored pillars, standing straight against the wind.

title: The Stone Pillars
text: Rising from the flat, rock-strewn plain are massive, stone-colored pillars, standing straight against the wind.
prev: You turn toward the horizon, and your eyes catch something impossible.

title: The Stone Pillars
text: They look like chimneys or telephone poles, casting long shadows across the low green carpet of moss.

title: The Stone Pillars
text: If you reached out to touch one, you would feel no rough bark and no sticky sap. So what was this silent giant?

title: Prototaxites
text: The fossils did look like weathered logs, and the name Prototaxites means first yew.
nxt: After all, what else could grow into a trunk eight meters tall? But as microscopes improved, a strange problem appeared.

title: Prototaxites

prev: The fossils did look like weathered logs, and the name Prototaxites means first yew.

title: Prototaxites
text: Where were the growth rings, and where were the plant cells?

title: Not Wood
text: When researchers sliced through the fossils, they found no wood fibers and no plant cell walls.

title: Not Wood
text: Instead, they found a dense, tightly woven mass of microscopic tubes, some hollow and some filled with thinner filaments.
nxt: This structure looked nothing like a tree.

title: Not Wood

title: Not Wood

nxt: Could the tallest organism on land, at the dawn of life on land, have been a gigantic fungus?

title: What a Fungus Is
text: To see why that is so strange, think about what a mushroom really is.
nxt: The mushroom you spotted in the moss is only the visible part, a fruiting body that exists to release spores.

title: What a Fungus Is
text: The real organism is hidden underground, a web of fine threads called hyphae, which together make up the mycelium.
nxt: These threads dissolve and absorb their food from the outside.

title: What a Fungus Is
text: Most fungi never grow large above ground, because soft threads and soft caps cannot hold up much weight.

title: What a Fungus Is
text: Fungi can still reach huge sizes, though.

title: The Great Debate
text: The idea sounded absurd.
nxt: Fungi are supposed to be soft, short-lived, and hidden in dark corners, not standing like stone monuments against the wind.

title: The Great Debate
text: In 2001, the paleobotanist Francis Hueber argued that these fossils were the remains of a giant fungus,
nxt: and the debate caught fire. For years, scientists argued.

title: The Great Debate
text: Some suggested a giant seaweed that had washed ashore. Others proposed a lichen, a partnership between a fungus and an alga.
nxt: Still others pictured a huge rolled-up mat of liverworts.

title: The Carbon Clue
text: Then came a clue from chemistry.
nxt: In 2007, geochemists measured the carbon isotopes preserved in Prototaxites fossils.

title: The Carbon Clue
text: In 2007, geochemists measured the carbon isotopes preserved in Prototaxites fossils.
prev: Then came a clue from chemistry.
nxt: Plants draw carbon straight from the air, so their isotope signatures stay fairly consistent.

title: The Carbon Clue
text: But the signatures in Prototaxites varied widely between specimens.
nxt: That fits an organism that was not making food from sunlight, but absorbing nourishment from whatever decaying matter surrounded it.

title: The Carbon Clue

title: A Giant Decomposer
text: That picture changed how we see this lost world. Prototaxites was probably not a tree sunbathing in the Silurian light.

title: A Giant Decomposer
text: It was more likely an immense decomposer, feeding on organic crusts, mats of early plants, and the remains of tiny microbes.

title: A Giant Decomposer
text: While modern molds spread invisible threads through damp bread or a basement wall, this ancient giant built a tower.

title: A Giant Decomposer
text: For roughly forty million years, from the Silurian into the Devonian, the tallest things on dry land were not plants or animals. They were very likely fungi.

text: Now a word of honesty, because science is never finished.

text: In 2025, a research team reported a preprint, not yet peer reviewed,
nxt: that found no trace of chitin, the material that normally builds fungal cell walls.

title: A Word of Honesty

title: A Quiet Plain
text: Picture that landscape at dusk. There is no grass, because grass would not evolve for hundreds of millions of years.
nxt: There are no flowers, no insects buzzing, and no dinosaurs.

title: A Quiet Plain
text: The only tall things in sight are these pale towers, each one standing alone, and each one older than anything a human has ever seen.

title: Life at the Foot
text: Have you ever wondered what life was like at the foot of such a giant?

title: Life at the Foot
text: Crawling around its base were some of the first land animals: tiny armored millipedes,
nxt: primitive springtails, and early relatives of spiders and scorpions.

text: To creatures this small, a single trunk was less a landmark than a mountain, and perhaps a source of shade, shelter, and moisture.

title: A Shelter?
text: In a world with no forests to cast deep shade, these towers may have offered shelter from harsh wind and strong ultraviolet light.

title: A Shelter?
text: They may have been a hub for fragile communities of tiny animals on an otherwise empty planet. But we should be careful here.
nxt: Fossil burrows show that animals used the trunks.

title: Why So Tall: Spores
text: Still, a bigger question lingers. Why would any living thing invest so much energy in a spire as tall as a two-story building?
nxt: One hypothesis is about reproduction.

title: Why So Tall: Spores

title: Why So Tall: Spores
text: Fungi release microscopic spores into the air and rely on breezes to carry their offspring.
nxt: Near the ground, friction slows the wind to a crawl.

title: Why So Tall: Water
text: Another hypothesis treats the tower as a storage tank.
nxt: In an early land environment with unpredictable rains and drying winds, holding on to water was a matter of life and death.

nxt: and carry the organism through a drought while the low mosses around it withered.

title: The First Trees
text: But the reign of the giants could not last forever. Beneath their shadow, a quiet revolution was beginning.
nxt: Green plants were no longer content to creep along the mud.

title: The First Trees
text: Over millions of years they developed rigid plumbing that could lift water upward,
nxt: tough compounds that stiffened their stems, and broad leaves that captured sunlight.

title: The First Trees
text: The first true trees, like Archaeopteris, appeared in the Devonian, around three hundred and eighty-five million years ago.

title: The First Trees
text: Their deep roots helped turn bare rock into soil, and they spread across the continents in dense forests.

title: The First Trees
text: The fungal towers, once alone on the horizon, were now standing in the shade of something taller.

title: The First Trees
text: Imagine looking up from the base of an eight-meter pillar and seeing a leafy crown high above you.

title: The First Trees
text: It must have been a very different world from the one the giants had known for tens of millions of years.

title: The Fall of the Giants
text: How could a fungal spire survive in a world of leafy crowns? Scientists suspect it could not.

title: The Fall of the Giants
text: Forest canopies cast deep shade over the surface crusts and mats that the giants may have fed on.

title: The Fall of the Giants
text: The new wood of the first trees was also tough, and fungi of the time may not yet have had the tools to break it down easily.

title: The Fall of the Giants
text: Whatever the exact cause, Prototaxites faded from the fossil record by the Late Devonian. The age of the fungal pillars was over.

title: Fungi Change Strategy
text: Yet this was not a defeat for fungi. Fungi did not vanish.

title: Fungi Change Strategy
text: Fungi as a whole kept going, and spread their thread-like networks, called mycelium,
nxt: through the dark, fertile soil, recycling the remains of the plants that had taken the sky.

title: Fungi Change Strategy
text: In fact, partnerships between fungi and plant roots are far older than forests.
nxt: Fossils from around four hundred million years ago already show fungi living inside the tissues of early land plants.

title: The Hidden Network
text: Scrape away the top layer of dirt in any woodland today, and you will meet the legacy of that transition.

title: The Hidden Network
text: Beneath your feet lies a hidden labyrinth of white threads wrapping around the roots of trees.
nxt: This underground system is called a mycorrhizal network.

title: The Hidden Network
text: This underground system is called a mycorrhizal network.
prev: Beneath your feet lies a hidden labyrinth of white threads wrapping around the roots of trees.

title: The Hidden Network
text: Fungi deliver minerals, nitrogen, and water from the soil to the roots. In return, trees send down sugars made in their sunlit leaves.

title: The Hidden Network
text: An ancient rivalry has become an alliance, and most of the plants on Earth depend on it.

title: Roles Reversed
text: Isn't it fascinating how history can flip the roles of living things?
nxt: Over four hundred million years ago, fragile plants cowered in the shadow of giant spires.

title: Roles Reversed
text: Over four hundred million years ago, fragile plants cowered in the shadow of giant spires.
prev: Isn't it fascinating how history can flip the roles of living things?

title: Roles Reversed
text: Today, enormous trees reach for the sun, while mushrooms pop up humbly around their trunks.

title: Roles Reversed
text: Yet without the fungal world below, breaking down dead wood and feeding roots, forests would choke under their own debris.

title: The Next Walk
text: The next time you walk through a quiet park, pause near a patch of moss.

title: The Next Walk
text: Look up at the oak or spruce above you, then look down at the small, pale mushroom beside your shoe.

title: The Next Walk
text: Beneath that quiet cap lies a lineage that reaches back to a forgotten chapter of our planet's history.

title: The Next Walk
text: Long before leaves whispered in the breeze, the world may have belonged to silent, towering spires, standing proud beneath a lonely sky.
nxt: Perhaps the giants never truly vanished.
